title: Parenting Styles and Intergenerational Transmission of Internet Addiction Risk: A Cross-Cultural Latent Class Analysis
abstract: Problematic internet use in early and middle adolescence (ages 12–15) is increasingly recognized as a family-level concern, yet little is known about whether internet addiction (IA) risk shows a similar underlying structure across generations and cultures. Using parent reports from 1,530 families across five countries, this study identified latent IA risk profiles based on ratings of both parents and their children and examined associations with parenting style and cultural context. Low, Moderate, and High IA Risk classes emerged for both parents and children. Profile structure was stable across countries, although prevalence varied. Parents rated children as having higher IA than themselves, and parent-child association was evident: High-risk parents were more likely to have High- or Moderate-risk children, whereas Low-risk parents were mainly linked with Low-risk children. Authoritative parenting was associated with lower risk, and authoritarian parenting with higher risk. These findings support profile-based IA assessment and culturally sensitive family interventions.
